newsitem.title: CUBA: Vatican foreign minister arrives in Cuba.
newsitem.headline: Vatican foreign minister arrives in Cuba.

text.p: Vatican Foreign Minister Jean Louis Tauran arrived in Cuba on a five-day visit that could pave the way for a meeting between Pope John Paul and President Fidel Castro and for a later papal visit to the communist-ruled island.
Tauran, who flew from Rome via Madrid, was met at Havana's Jose Marti airport by Foreign Minister Roberto Robaina.

Tauran is the first Vatican secretary for relations with foreign states to be invited to Cuba by the government. His visit comes at a time of improved relations between Cuba's communist authorities and the Roman Catholic Church.

The visit could help prepare for a meeting between Castro and the pope, if the Cuban leader goes to Rome for a World Food Summit organised by the U.N. Food and Agriculture Organisation from Nov. 13 to 17.

Diplomatic sources in Rome have said that if Castro does see the pope he would probably invite him to Cuba, perhaps next year. The island is the only Latin American country the pontiff has not visited.

Tauran is likely to meet Castro during his stay in Cuba, although this has not been officially confirmed. He is scheduled to meet a series of senior government leaders, as well as Cuba's Cardinal Jaime Ortega.
A Cuban Catholic Church magazine, Palabra Nueva, said in its October edition the church hoped the visit would help firm up the possibility of a papal visit.

While acknowledging that there is currently an improved relationship between the authorities and the church, the Foreign Ministry said on Friday, however, that Tauran's trip should not be seen as aimed at preparing any other visit.
"One should not attribute to this visit a characteristic of preparing for some other visit," ministry spokesman Miguel Alfonso told a weekly news briefing, in answer to a question.
Alfonso said the current relationship with the Vatican was "fairly good, with fluid communications, and this visit (by Tauran) gives us the chance to increase these contacts".
The spokesman noted with approval remarks last week by a senior Vatican cardinal, Roger Etchegeray, condemning widespread hunger in the world as an abuse of human rights.
In his comments Etchegeray also directly criticised a recent toughening of the longstanding U.S. embargo against Cuba.

Cuban authorities have moved in recent years to relax relations with the Christian churches, strained after the 1959 revolution that brought Castro to power. But tensions have persisted with the Catholic Church, in particular because of calls by the Catholic bishops for political change.
An improvement in ties in recent months was signalled by Cardinal Ortega in September when he said that comments about religion in a recent Communist Party document were encouraging.
